ASCG: Adaptive Spatial Classifier Guidance for Surgical Concept Suppression in Diffusion Models

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (144 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.20625v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: While text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models achieve remarkable quality, they risk producing harmful content. Existing safety mechanisms often rely on indiscriminate, global interventions that induce unintended semantic drift and degrade image quality. To address this, we propose Adaptive Spatial Classifier Guidance (ASCG), a necessity-driven framework that employs probabilistic monitoring to activate guidance selectively upon harm detection. By leveraging Grad-CAM for localized suppression, ASCG effectively removes harmful concepts while preserving superior semantic fidelity compared to conventional methods. Furthermore, we overcome the limitations of traditional metrics like NudeNet---which fails to assess semantic integrity---by introducing a VLM-based evaluation framework to provide a fine-grained, robust analysis of both safety and context preservation. Our results demonstrate that ASCG not only balances safety and fidelity but also exhibits remarkable plug-and-play synergy with existing frameworks to establish state-of-the-art performance.

#61268. Photonic Maxwells demon as an energy resource

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (203 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Photonic Maxwells demon as an energy resource

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (203 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.21972v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose a newly introduced realization of Maxwells demon for photons and its use as an energy resource. The starting point is a multilayer dielectric mirror that transmits photons within a certain wavelength band but reflects photons at longer wavelengths, followed by a material that irreversibly converts the wavelength. A 3D box constructed from these one-way mirrors is a self-acting Maxwells demon for photons. The first case considered is a one-way mirror for visible photons, converting blue to red as an example. The next case is a one-way mirror that transmits visible light but reflects infrared light, followed by a perfect blackbody. We analyze a 3D box with such mirrors as walls to accumulate and store blackbody radiation. Applications include solar-powered thermal energy and solar-powered thermophotovoltaics. The latter case would combine the 3D box with an ultra-low bandgap semiconductor photovoltaic cell inside. In the ideal optical limit, radiation can enter the box but cannot return through the entrance channel after conversion, allowing repeated photon recycling and nearly complete optical utilization. This can in principle move the conversion efficiency toward the thermodynamic limit for solar-energy conversion, the Landsberg limit of 93.3%.

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (265 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

OpenRoIS: A Community-Driven Open-Source Middleware Implementing the Robotic Interaction Service (RoIS) Framework for Physical Robots, Virtual Avatars, and Digital Services

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (265 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2609.21178v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Service applications for human-robot interaction are commonly written against the hardware-specific interfaces of one platform, so a change of hardware forces a rewrite. The Robotic Interaction Service (RoIS) Framework 2.0, standardized by the Object Management Group (OMG), addresses this fragmentation with a platform-independent model in which Service Applications drive Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) Engines through standardized interfaces and symbolic messages. A specification alone, however, does not provide the maintained implementation, Software Development Kits (SDKs), and adapters that adoption requires. This paper presents OpenRoIS, a community-driven open-source middleware that implements RoIS 2.0, and takes the position that an openly developed, paradigm-neutral implementation is what carries the standard into practice. OpenRoIS contributes a recursive engine for both the main and the sub HRI Engines, a single protocol in which the RoIS method catalog over JSON-RPC 2.0 and WebSocket is the only interface at every hop, a single-source type pipeline for three languages, client SDKs for JavaScript, Python, and Unity, a component SDK, a browser inspector, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for AI agents. These interfaces let a Service Application, scripted or an AI agent, address physical robots, virtual avatars, and digital services alike, each behind an adapter. In the functional validation, an AI agent and the browser inspector drove two physical robots from different vendors, a Reachy Mini and a Kachaka, behind one gateway, where a single command makes one robot greet a visitor while the other drives to the entrance. All of it is openly developed under the Apache-2.0 license at https://openrois.org/.

Let $(X, Y) \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times p}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be a sample and $W \in \mathbb{R}^{n_1\times n}$, $R \in \mathbb{R}^{p\times p_1}$ be two random projections. #61259. Navi-Agent: Unlocalized Monocular Navigation Agent

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (163 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Navi-Agent: Unlocalized Monocular Navigation Agent

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (163 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2609.20388v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Vision-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) requires an embodied agent to execute long-horizon instructions in unknown environments. Existing zero-shot VLN-CE systems typically maintain spatial states through geometric localization or coordinate-based representations. Recent geometry-constrained navigation removes depth and globally consistent coordinates, but maintaining persistent spatial awareness for place confirmation, progress verification, and recovery remains challenging. We present Navi-Agent, a zero-shot VLN-CE agent that constructs a coordinate-free spatial state from visual observations and executed motion histories. Navi-Agent organizes this state as a navigation topology, where nodes represent visual places and edges represent motion transitions. This representation enables observation-based approximate self-localization, task progress verification, and visual revisitation-based recovery. Navi-Agent performs closed-loop navigation by decomposing instructions into sub-goals, executing local visual navigation, and verifying visited places through the constructed spatial state. Experiments on zero-shot VLN-CE benchmark and real-world robot platforms show that Navi-Agent achieves state-of-the-art performance among geometry-constrained methods while remaining competitive with approaches relying on geometric localization.

#61255. HINT: Human-Intent Inception for Agentic Robot Manipulation

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (187 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

HINT: Human-Intent Inception for Agentic Robot Manipulation

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (187 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2609.02653v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Humans can perform complex manipulations given a simple intent through an overall instruction, while continuously adapting to evolving visual observations. However, current vision-language action (VLA) models and other action policies struggle to realize this high-level intelligent behavior under dense, evolving visual inputs and sparse language guidance. Visual correlations can then dominate semantic intent, leading actions to follow visual shortcuts rather than human goals. We present HINT (Human-INTent INcepTion), an agentic framework inspired by the human manipulation principles: semantic intent changes sparsely at manipulation-pattern transitions, whereas continuous control primarily depends on the evolving object-hand relationship. HINT invokes semantic reasoning only at pattern transitions to resolve the current subtask and target, then maintains this commitment through multi-view grounding and visual tracking. We explore two visual interfaces-image-space semantic highlighting and attention-prior injection-to communicate the tracked intent to the action policy without introducing additional trainable parameters into the foundation action model. Experiments across three long-horizon tasks and out-of-distribution variants show that HINT substantially improves intent understanding, task progress, and end-to-end success across two foundation policies while preserving low-latency control. Project page: https://robot-hint.github.io/.

#61253. Contact-Aided Factor-Graph Localization for Underwater Sampling

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (192 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Contact-Aided Factor-Graph Localization for Underwater Sampling

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (192 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Industry observers note that arXiv:2608.26932v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Accurate state estimation for autonomous underwater vehicles performing close-range seafloor sampling remains challenging. In low-altitude operation, down-looking cameras over featureless planar seabeds produce scale ambiguity, lateral degeneracy, and inconsistent feature tracking. Meanwhile, inertial-Doppler Velocity Log (DVL) fusion alone provides no mechanism for structural drift correction. We propose a Contact-Aided Factor-Graph Localization framework that treats physical interaction as an informative geometric constraint within a smoothing-based localization formulation. The method tightly fuses suction-based manipulator contact events with adaptive visual odometry, learned object detections, and on-board sensors. Visual odometry relative-pose factors and landmark bearing-range factors are uncertainty-scaled according to inlier statistics to prevent visually weak frames from destabilizing the estimator, while contact events are modeled as high-confidence factors that induce implicit loop closures without appearance-based place recognition. Furthermore, the system can fully initialize online during motion. Experimental evaluation in tanks, harbor, and simulation environments demonstrates that contact-induced constraints significantly reduce trajectory drift and improve object revisit accuracy compared to filtering-based navigation and contact-free graph formulations. These results highlight the role of embodied physical interaction as a localization primitive in perception-degraded underwater environments.

In a representative combined uncertainty/disturbance case, Cartesian RMS error was 0.0221419 m with CTC and 0.0128462 m with residual DDPG-CTC (approximately 42% lower). On a different circular reference, the residual branch nevertheless increased joint-limit-violating channel samples from 44 to 101. Separate supplemental experiments analyze training variability and checkpoints, alternative compensators, reward/action sensitivity, independently varied parameters and disturbances, trajectory transfer, constrained cable-force allocation and force lag. These studies show both improvements and failures, including early terminations and force-capacity-dependent degradation. The verified original algebraic force-backprojection path and later bounded-force simulations are distinguished; numerical allocations do not establish physical pretension or motor performance. Simscape and MSC ADAMS checks are numerical cross-model consistency assessments. No hardware, hardware-in-the-loop or patient tests were performed, and no clinical efficacy or physical safety guarantee is claimed.

Success rate combines reaching accuracy (endpoint error below 2 cm) and holding stability (variance below 2.5e-5 m^2). arXiv:2605.10931v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Transformers with self-attention modules as their core components have become an integral architecture in modern large language and foundation models. In this paper, we study the evolution of tokens in deep encoder-only transformers at inference time which is described in the large-token limit by a mean-field continuity equation. Leveraging ideas from the convergence analysis of interacting multi-particle systems, with particles corresponding to tokens, we prove that the token distribution rapidly concentrates onto the push-forward of the initial distribution under a projection map induced by the key, query, and value matrices, and remains metastable for moderate times. Specifically, we show that the Wasserstein distance of the two distributions scales like $\sqrt{{\log(\beta+1)}/{\beta}}\exp(Ct)+\exp(-ct)$ in terms of the temperature parameter $\beta^{-1}\to 0$ and inference time $t\geq 0$. For the proof, we establish Lyapunov-type estimates for the zero-temperature equation, identify its limit as $t\to\infty$, and employ a stability estimate in Wasserstein space together with a quantitative Laplace principle to couple the two equations. Our result implies that for time scales of order $\log\beta$, which correspond to the early-phase behavior most relevant for practical finite-depth models, the token distribution concentrates at the identified limiting distribution. Numerical experiments confirm this and, beyond that, complement our theory by showing that for finite $\beta$ and large $t$ the dynamics enter a different terminal phase, dominated by the spectrum of the value matrix.

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.21855v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study shortest-path percolation on spatial networks that model the quantum internet based on optical fibers. In this process, the removal of paths describes the consumption of the entangled links used for communication. We compare finite and unrestricted path-length bounds for networks whose average degree either increases with system size or remains approximately constant. We show that networks become more robust as the average degree increases, whereas networks with approximately constant average degree exhibit a data collapse for the fixed finite bounds considered. Using Monte Carlo sampling of the shortest-path-length distribution, we estimate an equivalent path cost, a finite bound that approximately reproduces the degradation of the network in the unrestricted case. For networks with fixed average degree, this cost grows approximately as the square root of the number of nodes. Increasing the bound beyond this value requires additional computation time without appreciably changing the percolation dynamics. As a complementary result, for Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi random networks, we find an empirical relation between the initial average degree and the approximately common crossing point of the percolation curves for different path-length bounds.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (213 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.20433v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scene chronology aims to reconstruct a scene across visits separated by hours or days, during which objects may change in position, presence or shape. Such reconstruction must retain every earlier state, yet each revisit often provides only a few images. Storing a complete model for each visit duplicates the unchanged scene, whereas updating a single shared model alters earlier states. We present ReScene, which stores each visit as an immutable compact update, so that any earlier visit can be recovered exactly by applying the stored updates in order, without retaining past images. To localise each update, ReScene attributes the disagreement between the preceding reconstruction and the fresh images to individual Gaussians through their compositing weights. This attribution guides the suppression of outdated Gaussians and the refinement of persistent ones, while newly visible surfaces are initialised from learned multi-view depth. We also introduce Multi-State, a benchmark of non-rigid deformation and partial material removal, including synthetic scenes with ground-truth geometry. ReScene achieves quality higher than sequential 3DGS checkpointing with 2.5--4.8$\times$ less uncompressed history storage. At comparable PSNR, it also reduces foreground depth error by 3.2$\times$ relative to sequential ChronoGS, showing that accurate rendering does not necessarily imply accurate geometry. Code and benchmark are available at https://waychin-weiqin.github.io/ReScene/.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2608.13438v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Contact-rich manipulation failures are often detected only after the robot has committed to contact. This is especially limiting in wrist-camera setups: close gripper--object views help observe contact, but a poor approach may already push, miss, slip, or disturb the object before conventional detectors react. We introduce ContactGuard, a pre-contact execution monitor for chunked visuomotor policies. Given the policy's planned action chunk, ContactGuard predicts its short-horizon consequence in latent visual space and aborts if the predicted future latent indicates likely failure. Its latent world model is trained from unlabelled robot trajectories to predict compact multi-view visual embeddings under planned actions, avoiding pixel-level video prediction. A lightweight failure probe is then trained from a small labelled set of pre-contact clips. At deployment, ContactGuard anchors prediction before an imminent contact event, rolls the model forward under the policy's own actions, and verifies the predicted post-contact latent. Across real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, ContactGuard consistently benefits from action-conditioned latent prediction over current-state and direct-prediction alternatives. Counterfactual action perturbations further show that its failure score responds to the specific action being proposed. We deploy the same frozen monitor online with the visuomotor policy, where it provides a pre-contact abort signal without modifying the underlying policy.

Prior work has primarily focused on improving absolute accuracy in transfer learning. In this work, we systematically study the robustness of quantum models under reduced training data. We evaluate multiple quantum and classical architectures across diverse transfer tasks and retraining configurations, and quantify robustness using accuracy degradation and relative performance retention (RPR). Our results show that, although classical models often achieve higher peak performance, they exhibit significantly larger degradation when training data is limited. Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.21745v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Two-dimensional electrons in a strong magnetic field exhibit two seemingly incompatible ground states: incompressible quantum Hall liquids with a quantized Hall conductance, and electron crystals in which interactions drive the charge into ordered patterns. Moir\'e superlattices in transition-metal-dichalcogenide bilayers offer a tunable arena for this competition. Using neural quantum states (NQS) together with several methodological advances, we show how this competition unfolds. In particular, we demonstrate that the two end points are separated by an extended regime in which molecular charge order coexists with a quantized Hall response. We map the ground-state phase diagram of electrons at Landau-level filling $\nu_B=1$ in the presence of a moir\'e superlattice potential, with three electrons per moir\'e cell. In the deep triangular potential limit, the electrons form the topologically trivial "Wigner molecular crystal'' of three-electron artificial atoms, a state recently imaged at zero magnetic field in moir\'e bilayers. As the potential depth is lowered, molecular charge order remains while quantized Hall response emerges. At the honeycomb point, where each cell contains three electrons and two degenerate moir\'e minima, wells are either singly or doubly occupied and the doublons provide an emergent Ising degree of freedom. Starting from modest interaction strength, we find short-range doublon correlations within the Chern insulator which grow with interaction strength and eventually break sublattice symmetry, forming a N\'eel CDW with long-range order between doublons. The topological molecular regime lies at twist angles and magnetic fields directly accessible to current experiments. The methodological advances presented provide a scalable framework for exploring a broad range of questions in correlated quantum matter in the presence of magnetic fields.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.20385v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Can a vision-language model look at a picture of a chain reaction and tell what will happen? Recent multimodal models describe scenes fluently and solve textbook physics problems, which suggests they should also predict how a scene of ramps, ledges, pendulums, seesaws and dominoes plays out once a ball is pushed. We tested this claim on 30 models from 10 families and reached a clear conclusion: unaided, no model predicts the outcome reliably. We built DominoBench, a benchmark of still images of 2D rigid-body scenes whose outcome a physics simulator computes. It holds 854 items in 427 minimal pairs, in which a change of one to three grid steps in one quantity decides whether one person survives, and every item comes with a four-rung hint ladder ending in the exact calculation that decides the outcome. Unaided, frontier models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI are right about the person whose fate flips in at most 75% of items and answer both twins of a pair correctly in at most 40%. Pointing at the deciding step helps little, and exact geometry given as text barely helps, yet once the deciding calculation and the quantities it needs, including speeds that a still image cannot show, are written out, the same models reach 80-92% on the deciding person, while small open-weight models stay near chance. Physical prediction from a still image therefore fails at the quantitative step: the strongest models use the deciding quantity when they are given it, but do not produce it on their own. For models that plan or act in the physical world, a fluent account of a scene is thus no evidence of a correct prediction: such models must find and compute the deciding quantity unprompted, and DominoBench tests whether they do.

arXiv:2607.26817v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Visual Floorplan Localization (FLoc) has emerged as a promising solution for indoor localization by matching egocentric images against minimalist structural maps. However, due to cross-modal information asymmetry and repetitive indoor layouts, visual FLoc is fundamentally challenged by multimodal pose distributions, where visually identical observations map to distinct, spatially separated locations. Existing ray-matching-based methods tackle this by explicitly predicting sparse geometric or semantic rays, which inherently incur information loss and demand resource-intensive preprocessing alongside exhaustive matching during inference. In this paper, we bypass the intermediate ray-matching paradigm and propose a coarse-to-fine visual FLoc framework that progresses from uncertainty to determinism. In the coarse stage, we design an image-conditioned pose diffusion model to parameterize the continuous multimodal pose distribution, effectively routing stochastically initialized pose particles toward distinct candidate modes. In the refinement stage, we propose a localized refiner that predicts bounded sub-meter pose residuals from candidate-centered floorplan crops, where structural ambiguities are largely eliminated. Our method effectively balances global multi-hypothesis tracking and local sub-meter refinement without requiring any offline map preprocessing or test-time lookup tables. Comprehensive results on the S3D (full) and ZInD benchmarks demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and robustness.

arXiv:2611.20349v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Is a face or a voice still heard once the words are known? Incomplete multimodal learning increasingly uses large language models (LLMs) as fusion engines: modality features enter as token blocks and missing modalities become placeholders. We find that LLM-driven fusion can override non-verbal evidence it can read. Contrasting its full-input prediction with counterfactual views, the same model shown one modality or no content, we identify language shortcuts. We build MR-Bench: MR-Bench-A types every test sample of four sentiment benchmarks; MR-Bench-H contains 900 human-validated clips (620 language-shortcut, LS; 280 non-verbal-shortcut, NS) from seven sources, and every model is scored on all of them. Zero-shot MLLMs solve at most 32.7% of the LS clips; adding the transcript to the muted video lowers vision-language accuracy by 46.1-53.1 points. Yet inverting a text-only model's answers solves 94.4%, so LS accuracy alone cannot establish use of non-verbal evidence. Inside the fusion LLM, fused states align increasingly with the text view late in the decoder. Counterfactual-View Reliability learning (CoVeR) trains views as unimodal judges and withholds fused supervision where they disagree. It achieves state-of-the-art results on five benchmarks without extra inference cost in accuracy mode. On MR-Bench-H, it reaches 61.7% LS and 93.6% NS accuracy; robust mode raises LS accuracy to 63.0% while lowering NS accuracy to 84.8%. Among LS clips solved without text, adding text causes errors on 30.1% with CoVeR versus 32.2% with LLM-Fusion. Project page: https://peacelwh.github.io/CoVeR/.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2511.18820v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present a physics-constrained neural solver for incompressible flow that requires neither labeled data nor supervised pretraining. The solver enforces incompressibility and boundary conditions (BCs) to strict tolerances. We attribute the limited Reynolds numbers of existing physics-informed approaches to insufficient enforcement of these constraints, on which conventional finite-difference and finite-volume solvers depend. We therefore formulate incompressible flow as a constrained optimization problem within the physics- and equality-constrained artificial neural network (PECANN) framework: the pressure Poisson residual is minimized subject to the momentum equations, continuity equation, and BCs imposed as equality constraints on the primitive variables, while a conditionally adaptive augmented Lagrangian method enforces each constraint. The pressure Poisson objective proves critical. Across all benchmarks, replacing it with the momentum residual fails to converge to accurate solutions under identical architecture and constraint enforcement, which we attribute to the global elliptic coupling of pressure and velocity that local momentum-residual minimization lacks. For advection-dominated flows, we introduce an adaptive vanishing entropy viscosity that stabilizes training while leaving the converged solution unchanged. The solver predicts lid-driven cavity flow up to Re = 7,500 with centerline velocity profiles matching benchmark data, and is further validated on flow over a backward-facing step at Re = 800, 3D unsteady Beltrami flow, and steady and unsteady flow past a circular cylinder under an inflow-outflow configuration, for which an ablation study identifies admissible outlet BCs for velocity and pressure. From a randomly initialized network and without external perturbations, the solver captures the spontaneous onset of periodic vortex shedding in unsteady cylinder flow.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.20090v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Masked modeling is the dominant self-supervised paradigm for point-cloud videos. However, it leaks the information it is meant to predict, whether it reconstructs masked points as in MAE-style methods or predicts their latent features. Because point-cloud tokens are anchored at points sampled from each frame, querying a target at its own position reveals where its geometry has moved, in reconstruction and latent prediction alike. For latent predictors, random spatio-temporal masks introduce a further shortcut, as visible frames on both sides of each target allow interpolation rather than forecasting. The pretext task thus reduces to completion. Once the target positions are withheld, a masked latent predictor performs only slightly better than copying the last frame. To remove this leakage, we propose PointWM, a latent world model that turns completion into forecasting by predicting the features and geometry of future frames from strictly earlier context. Each target is queried only with its last-seen position and timestamp, while a latent action learned without annotations is meant to capture the part of the future that the past leaves undetermined. On HOI4D action segmentation with a P4Transformer backbone, PointWM improves F1@50 over training from scratch by 24.9 offline and 29.1 under strictly causal inference. These results show the promise of latent world models as a leakage-free pretraining paradigm for point-cloud videos.Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/InitalZ/PointWM.

We propose Gradient-free Robot Action generation via Combined diffusion-MPPI posterior mean Estimation (GRACE), which guides a pretrained diffusion policy with Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control using only forward cost evaluations. This framework enables exact Neyman-Pearson tests by training the target model on samples from another tractable surrogate, which is itself trained on real data. We argue that the EPiC-FM generative model is a valid surrogate reference for JetClass jets and apply SURF to show that modern jet taggers may already be operating close to the true statistical limit. By contrast, we find that autoregressive GPT models unphysically exaggerate top vs. QCD separation power encoded in the surrogate reference, implying that they are giving a misleading picture of the fundamental limit.

On hardware, MorphQuad preserves a planar quadrotor structure, and independently articulates each of the four rotor systems, eliminating control singularities and enabling all rotors to align and vector the platform's maximum thrust in any direction; on control and thrust allocation, MorphQuad enjoys a closed-form null-space correction for gimbal lock and downwash interference that maintains almost-everywhere stability via coupling with a generalized geometric controller. With fully-onboard computation, localization, and trajectory execution, MorphQuad demonstrates continuous multi-revolution rotation while translating or hovering (maneuverability); valve turning, perching, and object pressing and pushing with human-wrist strength (manipulation); and push-pull recovery and wind rejection, even when directed to a single rotor (resiliency).

We are interested in asking: can a single perception representation support different levels of understanding without being designed for any specific task? By modeling the spatial existence and semantics of the environment, it naturally bridges different perception granularities, from coarse scene understanding to fine-grained object localization. Therefore, we introduce AerialOcc, a unified occupancy-based perception model that enables multiple drone perception tasks from a single inference process, without maintaining task-specific prediction heads. To facilitate this direction, we construct AerialOcc-20K, a large-scale multi-class occupancy dataset for aerial environments. Extensive experiments show that AerialOcc achieves competitive performance across diverse perception tasks while preserving a unified architecture. Our findings demonstrate that occupancy can serve as a universal perception interface, offering a latest perspective toward flexible and scalable visual intelligence for autonomous drones from a common 3D scene representation. Finite-stiffness impedance control retains a static deflection there, while predictive alternatives typically optimize a nonlinear model online. Operational-space cancellation instead exposes a translational error double integrator with a fixed transition matrix and a configuration-scheduled input map, making interaction a predictive quantity. We build on it a compact offset-free interaction-error MPC for torque-controlled manipulators: a force-domain random-walk state estimates persistent interaction and model error, and a 30-variable convex QP maps the correction through the current task inertia while constraining the applied joint torque. Conditional results establish impedance equivalence of the unconstrained passive feedback, offset-free regulation at feasible frozen configurations, and quadratic stabilizability of the scheduled backbone. In a 1 kHz MuJoCo simulation of a 7-DOF Franka FR3, the estimator cuts steady-state error under a repeated 15 N step from 2.73 mm to 0.033 mm when added to the otherwise identical 100 Hz MPC, at unchanged peak joint power. A stiffness-and-damping-calibrated impedance baseline attains 2.63 mm at the same actuator cost, and 1.36 mm with ideal measured-force cancellation, so constant-load rejection is not unique to MPC; the sensorless controller still reaches 0.033 mm. The torque constraint holds the command inside a budget tightened to the lowest the task can meet, at no tracking cost. On a physical UR5e, five alternated pairs under a nominal 1.5 kg hanging load give 1.505 mm without the estimator; with it the controller is offset-free, its 0.023 mm error being the noise level of the encoder-based position measurement. A tuned anti-windup integral also removes the offset, with larger transients.

Here we show that the imaginary component of the extended Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobability reveals dynamical distinctions absent from out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs) formed from two repeated Hermitian observables at infinite temperature. We interpret its real and imaginary components as complementary quadratures of interference between many-body echo amplitudes. We prove that the imaginary component vanishes for every unitary evolution if either projective measurement has two outcomes, whereas nonreal values arise for generic unitary dynamics when it has at least three (e.g., spin-1 systems). We develop an algorithm to reconstruct the full quasiprobability from covariances of local probe signals over repeated preparations of randomised initial states, using forward evolution and probe readout only. In a spin-1 chain, a nonzero imaginary signal distinguishes a real Hamiltonian $H$ from $-H$ despite identical corresponding OTOCs, and identifies opposite sides of a pair-conversion resonance at short times while dipolar and quadrupolar OTOCs remain nearly unchanged. We establish that this service, which covers 85,000 species from around the world, (1) has a species prediction accuracy of 0.89, (2) process images up to 666 times faster than workflows requiring human intervention, (3) and has processed over 84 million identification requests since its launch, including more than 40 million in 2025 alone. We demonstrate how it has already enabled the implementation of a latest generation of ecological workflows. Finally, we illustrate its application using a reproducible example: identifying plants from insect photos on iNaturalist. 4. In conclusion, this machine-to-machine species identification is already operating on a considerable scale and meets a genuine need. All of this paves the way for a new paradigm in biodiversity monitoring, in which automated sensors and image collections can be directly connected to AI-based identification services.

arXiv:2611.18868v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) results for intensive care unit (ICU) time series are hard to compare when data processing, encoders, and adaptation vary together. We present SLICES, a benchmark and evaluation framework for comparing and extending SSL methods under a shared clinical setup. It fixes 24-hour value and observation-mask inputs, a Transformer encoder, patient-level splits, four endpoints, two adaptation protocols, and five matched seeds across MIMIC-IV, eICU-CRD, and their pooled union. Masked autoencoding (MAE), joint-embedding prediction (JEPA), and contrastive learning provide reference implementations. Among these objectives, MAE leads mean AUPRC in all nine frozen classification comparisons, also under converged probes, and in seven of nine fine-tuning comparisons. Fine-tuned MAE leads hospital mortality at full labels and scores higher than a supervised Transformer of the same architecture at every label fraction, and SSL fine-tuning gives the lowest length-of-stay error. Supervised baselines remain strong elsewhere: GRU-D leads 24-hour mortality and XGBoost leads acute kidney injury in all three regimes. Rankings depend on the adaptation protocol, the comparator set, and whether the probe loss matches the metric. A two-seed MIMIC-IV rerun with the maintained code stays within two across-seed SDs of the reference in all 48 downstream runs. The code repository supports latest objectives, shared downstream evaluation, and regeneration of the reference results, so new SSL methods can be compared with these references under the same conditions. Generalization to unseen hospitals is not tested here and is the natural next extension.

In the superradiant phase of the QRM with coupling strength above the critical point, the bosonic ground state exhibits temporally stable quantum non-Gaussian features. However, the quantum non-Gaussian features of such superradiant ground states can be fragile against loss during preparation. Here, we show that persistent quantum non-Gaussian features can instead be realized below the critical point through weak periodic qubit modulation. We analyze an adiabatic ramp protocol in which the modulation amplitude is gradually increased, allowing the system to approximately follow the instantaneous Floquet state. When the modulation period is tuned close to Poincar\'e-Birkhoff resonances, the resulting state exhibits pronounced quantum non-Gaussian features in the directly measurable Wigner function with a complex phase-space structure that is considerably more robust against loss than that of the superradiant ground state. The protocol of adiabatic ramps provides an attractive route for generating long-lived quantum non-Gaussian effects below the critical point.

arXiv:2611.16400v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: An assistant watching a worker can prepare for an emerging need before the worker is ready to receive help. As the need evolves, the assistant must maintain preparation until a response is due, or withdraw it if the need disappears. Video anticipation and interactive response benchmarks leave this interval between early evidence and response largely unmeasured. We introduce FuGIBench (Future-Grounded Interaction), a streaming-video benchmark in which a model chooses among waiting, reversible preparation, and response given a causal video prefix and a task contract. The benchmark contains 19,893 synthetic tool-assistance videos across ten tool tasks, in handover, ordinary-activity, and cancelled-need tracks. One primary score credits sustained preparation, incorporates response-interval alignment, and penalizes activity when the reference prescribes waiting. On a frozen set of 1,000 episodes, a reference system with a longer preparation lead has poorer response alignment, while similar handover leads accompany different levels of activity during ordinary work in matched scenarios. Together with cancellation analyses, these results show why evaluating preparation requires tracking decisions as needs develop, become actionable, or disappear.

Asymptotic Margins and Feature Confinement in Conic Classification Heads under Softmax Cross-Entropy

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (236 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.18507v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Classification heads built on conic functions give each class a bounded region of the feature space, and such regions are used to reject samples of unseen classes. We ask whether these regions also keep the features bounded when the head is trained with softmax cross-entropy. For a head whose class scores combine a linear term with a Euclidean norm, we first show that the region of each class is bounded by a quadric of revolution, whose eccentricity is the reciprocal of one learned ratio. We then attach to each class an asymptotic margin, which compares the growth of its score with the growth of all the other scores and can be computed by a second-order cone program. The loss of a class has infimum zero exactly when its margin is positive, and it then approaches zero only along diverging features. When the margin is negative, the loss is coercive and its minimizers lie in an explicit ball. Since softmax depends only on the differences between scores, a class with a bounded region can still have a positive margin, so bounded regions do not confine the features. The result extends to other norms, including the polyhedral conic functions. On CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, all 1210 cells of 67 trained conic heads have positive margins, whereas a prototype head keeps nine of its ten cells bounded, as the theory predicts.

arXiv:2611.08879v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing imagery provides rich spatial details but poses challenges for accurate and efficient multimodal understanding. Existing evidence acquisition methods selectively explore relevant image regions, yet largely rely on generative multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for intermediate search control. However, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) primarily aligns these models with human-preferred responses rather than explicitly optimizing region-level relevance judgments, while repeated autoregressive decoding introduces additional computational overhead. To address these limitations, we propose GeoJeV, a training-free method that formulates evidence acquisition as spatial probability-driven decision making. At each evaluated region, a frozen JeV model produces a probability distribution over candidate regions. Specifically, Region Rank prioritizes candidate regions, Sparse Branch adaptively determines branching width through sparse probability support, and Depth Gate controls refinement depth based on branch sparsity and distribution concentration. By coordinating search priority, branching width, and refinement depth through a shared distribution, GeoJeV reduces reliance on RLHF-aligned generation and eliminates intermediate decoding. Experiments on LRS-GRO, MME-RealWorld-RS, and LRS-VQA achieve accuracies of 60.59%, 52.79%, and 34.32%, respectively. Across the three benchmarks, GeoJeV improves the average accuracy of Qwen3-VL-8B by +5.32pp with only 1.12 additional seconds per question, while achieving a 7.8-fold inference speedup over the recent method.

A position measurement on the pointer induces a nonunitary conditional transformation of the qubit, allowing its post-measurement state to move along a trajectory on the Bloch sphere. We derive the conditional state, the measurement-outcome distribution, and the corresponding Bloch-sphere coordinates. For a real Gaussian pointer, the conditional state follows a meridian, whereas a phase-engineered Gaussian pointer produces a trajectory with a measurement-dependent azimuthal angle. We further describe outcome-dependent unitary feedback for preparing a prescribed target state from a known initial qubit state. We distinguish this state-preparation task from implementing a universal deterministic single-qubit gate, which does not follow from the proposed interaction and measurement alone. Finally, we derive the quantum Fisher information of the joint qubit--pointer state for estimating the displacement-generating parameter and discuss the implications of pointer squeezing, phase engineering, and experimental implementation. The results provide a framework for analysing conditional Bloch-sphere steering using continuous-variable measurement resources.

arXiv:2611.18239v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A unified framework is proposed that characterizes supervised deep classification as the decoding of error-correcting codes in the Shannon sense. Cross-entropy optimization is shown to align softmax classifiers with maximum-likelihood decoding, where logits map to Hamming distances to class-specific codewords. Unlike classical Error-Correcting Output Codes, deep networks are shown to learn effective codebooks in the feature space implicitly. Finally, this perspective is extended to self-supervised encoders, offering a cohesive explanation for the geometry of latent representations in modern neural models.

Industry News: Simulation-Informed Diffusion for Decentralized Multi-robot Motion Planning

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (205 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2605.27697v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Decentralized multi-robot motion planning requires each robot to generate collision-free trajectories from local observations, without global sensing or reliable communication. However, most existing planners, whether classical or learning-based, generate trajectories from a static snapshot of the local observation, which limits their ability to anticipate the future behavior of neighboring robots. This limitation is critical as the number of robots increases and the environment becomes more cluttered. Motivated by world models that use future state estimation to improve planning decisions, this paper introduces Simulation-Informed Diffusion (SID), a decentralized framework built on constraint-aware diffusion models (CADM) that simulate neighboring robots' future trajectories to guide each robot's own planning. SID first uses CADM to simulate the future trajectories of neighboring robots from their currently observed states, and then uses the same CADM to strategy each robot's own trajectory under safety constraints informed by these simulations. Crucially, the accurate simulation of neighbors enables a minimal communication scheme that triggers coordination only when necessary in highly congested scenarios. Experiments across diverse environments show that SID consistently outperforms baseline methods in terms of planning effectiveness and constraint satisfaction, and scales to scenarios with 108 robots and 160 obstacles.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2605.26304v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Collaborative navigation of heterogeneous robots in unknown environments poses significant challenges due to sensing, communication, and computational limitations. In this work, a lead robot navigates toward a target with the assistance of a mobile sensor robot (e.g., an airborne drone), whose task is to explore the environment and communicate relevant map information under bandwidth constraints. We propose a framework in which the sensor determines both which map regions to transmit and which navigation action to execute online, while also predicting unexplored regions of the environment. To this end, we present $\beta$-Sparse Gaussian Processes, a variational sparse Gaussian Process (GP) model for task-aware inducing point selection under cardinality constraints. Furthermore, we develop an action-selection strategy that balances task relevance with exploration. Simulations on Mars and Earth maps show that the proposed framework outperforms all considered bandwidth-constrained baselines, reducing accumulated path cost by approximately 35% compared to no communication, while decreasing transmitted information by 94% relative to the full-information GP baseline. The results further highlight the benefits of GP-based map prediction over methods without prediction, as well as the advantages of navigation-aware region selection over approaches that do not prioritize task-relevant regions.

Hands provide a natural interface, but translating continuous hand movements into coherent visual responses remains challenging because of complex hand-object dynamics and demanding real-time computation. To address these challenges, we introduce LynnReal-Hand, a hand-controlled video world model that unifies precise interaction modeling with efficient streaming generation. We curate 100K interaction clips spanning diverse real and synthetic environments and develop hand-aware supervision to improve fine-grained hand motions and object interactions. Building on this foundation, we learn a causal flow map for few-step generation and introduce region-aware score distillation that combines complementary video and image priors to refine interaction dynamics and visual appearance. To further reduce inference latency, we propose Ultra-Fast-VAE, a compact video decoder that preserves high reconstruction fidelity with substantially lower computational cost. Extensive evaluations on HandBench demonstrate superior hand-following accuracy and visual quality compared with existing approaches. Our full-sequence model achieves an FVD of 181.67 and a MANO Dice score of 93.02, while the three-step causal model maintains a MANO Dice score of 92.49. For real-time interaction, 540p streaming on a single H200 reaches 18.03 FPS with 741ms latency and an optimized peak GPU memory footprint of only 34.89GB. We will release the datasets, model weights, and the full training and inference code to support research on hand-controlled video world models.

arXiv:2611.15584v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Industrial plasma process development requires broad exploration of operating and geometric parameters. Geometric parameters, particularly electrode spacing, affect discharge structure and processing uniformity. Exploring these parameter spaces through repeated high-fidelity simulations can be computationally expensive. Surrogate models can offer rapid predictions, but geometric variation complicates their application because the computational domain and discretization may change across samples. In this work, six geometry-aware surrogate models based on prescribed and learned geometry mappings, extended-domain representation, continuous coordinates, and geometry-native discretizations are compared in terms of their data requirements for accurate predictions of full plasma fields and ion density profiles near the wafer. The simulation dataset spans pressure, voltage, frequency, and electrode gap, with each reference case requiring an average simulation cost of 5.32 CPU h. To achieve a 2% mean error across the four plasma fields, prescribed-mapping Geo-FNO and Transolver require 100 training cases, compared with 250-1000 for the other models. Predicting ion density profiles near the wafer is more demanding and reveals larger differences among models, with prescribed-mapping Geo-FNO requiring the fewest training cases for the profile accuracy targets considered. To further reduce the data required for accurate predictions near the wafer, we introduce charge-separation weighting into the training loss, which reduces the prescribed-mapping Geo-FNO's minimum tested training requirement for a 5% profile error from 1000 to 100 cases. These results support prescribed-mapping Geo-FNO as a practical starting point for the variable-gap problem studied here when a suitable geometry mapping is available, while Transolver achieves the highest prediction accuracy with sufficient training data.

Industry News: Quantum speed limits from symmetries: A numerical analysis

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (268 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.22630v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Target-specific quantum speed limits (QSLs) bound the minimal time required to realize a given operation. Recent theoretical work derives these limits directly from the symmetries of the dynamical Lie algebra of the control system and a symmetry-restoring perturbation, bypassing the need to solve the equations of motion. In practice, however, identifying a suitable symmetry and a perturbation that restores it demands strong physical intuition and offers no guarantee of tightness. We show that, for any given symmetry, the minimal restoring perturbation is the solution of a convex semidefinite program, which can be solved to global optimality and thus yields the tightest achievable speed limit for that symmetry. This semidefinite program is one building block of our numerical method, alongside an explicit computation of the space of admissible symmetries and a search over this space. Since this search is non-convex, it is addressed with gradient-based optimization, black-box heuristics, or the injection of physically motivated candidate symmetries. We apply the method to three examples: a two-qubit CNOT gate, a SWAP on a spinless-particle chain, and a Dicke state preparation on a qubit ring. Our results improve on previously known symmetry-based bounds, most notably for the SWAP, where solving the semidefinite program for the known analytical symmetry tightens the bound by a factor of approximately 2.5. For the Dicke state preparation, however, the bounds decrease with system size, which we trace back to a symmetry-independent perturbation ceiling. This work provides a reproducible numerical procedure for constructing target-specific quantum speed limits directly from the system Hamiltonians and the target operation.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2605.14598v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Diffusion-based imitation learning has shown strong promise for robot manipulation. However, most existing policies condition only on the current observation or a short window of recent observations, limiting their ability to resolve history-dependent ambiguities in long-horizon tasks. To address this, we introduce \ours, a history-conditioned Diffusion State Space Policy that enables efficient, full-history conditioning for robot manipulation. Leveraging the continuous sequence modeling properties of State Space Models (SSMs), our history encoder effectively compresses the entire observation stream into a compact context representation. To ensure this context preserves critical information regarding future state evolution, the encoder is optimized with a dynamics-aware auxiliary training objective. This high-level context representation is then seamlessly fused with recent state observations to form a hierarchical conditioning mechanism for action generation. Furthermore, to maintain architectural consistency and minimize GPU memory overhead, we also instantiate the diffusion backbone itself using an SSM. Extensive experiments across simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks show that \ours achieves state-of-the-art performance with a significantly smaller model size, demonstrating superior efficiency of the hierarchical conditioning in capturing crucial information as the history length increases. In 2D, FNO and U-Net each reach 1% interior error with 100 cases; FNO and Transolver each reach 2% parameter-boundary error with 200 cases, compared with 400 for U-Net. At the stricter 1% 2D parameter-boundary target, Transolver requires 400 cases versus 800 for FNO. Additional analyses investigate FNO spectral modes and padding, U-Net skip connections, Transolver adaptive slicing, and PCA-Net projection versus prediction error. The results support FNO as a data-efficient baseline for the tested CCP settings, while showing that the preferred architecture depends on the accuracy target and operating-parameter region.

Their DAVIS hole warping error is two to four times that of ProPainter, and copying along clean-video tracks lowers their recoverable LPIPS by a quarter to two fifths. EGS closes 43% and 56% of the gap to this copy reference on held-out DAVIS when its colors come from clean-video tracks. With colors tracked on the masked input, a pre-registered confirmation finds no gain on MiniMax-Remover and a loss on ROSE. Diffusion removers thus leave observed content unused on DAVIS, and training-free reuse does not yet hold with tracked evidence.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.22621v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Symmetric circuits require every symmetry of the input to extend to an automorphism of the circuit. In the classical setting, their connection to descriptive complexity yields strong unconditional lower bounds. We extend this approach to the quantum model of symmetric computation defined by Castro-Silva, Gur, and Strelchuk (ITCS 2026), proving a tradeoff between circuit size and entanglement width (the smallest $b$ such that, on every computational-basis input, the state after each layer factors into states on at most $b$ qubits each). Our main result identifies a graph property decidable in classical polynomial time that no polynomial-size family of symmetric quantum circuits on $n$-vertex graphs with entanglement width $o(n/\log n)$ can compute. The bound holds for circuits with arbitrary one-qubit and two-qubit gates and unrestricted depth, and remains valid under the weaker notion of symmetry with respect to even permutations of vertices. Our proof is based on a new quantum pebble game based on the partial trace. The resulting indistinguishability theorem transfers classical pebble-game lower bounds to quantum circuits with restricted entanglement. By contrast, without entanglement restrictions, we show that every graph property in BQP can be computed by a uniform family of polynomial-size symmetric quantum circuits. Restricting to circuits with no entanglement at all, we show that polynomial-size symmetric quantum circuits with entanglement width 1 can compute every graph property definable in fixed-point logic with counting. Finally, we give an efficient symmetric implementation of QAOA for MAX 3XOR, providing a starting point for studying entanglement lower bounds in quantum optimization algorithms.

RUO also needs fewer bits for tiny objects than the AV1 Image File Format (AVIF), High Efficiency Video Coding (HEVC) and three published learned codecs, and its advantage over threshold-based ROI coding persists when the sender and receiver use different detectors. It succeeds only on COCO and fails on the other four. We analyze the failures and find that alignment must first locate the subspace where the modalities co-vary and then orient the mapping within it. Consistent with previous studies, medical imaging is the hardest case: its shared subspace carries the smallest fraction of the variance. When this fraction is small, alignment needs image-text pairs, and random-matrix theory predicts how many pairs are needed. These findings motivate LightAlign: a few pairs let a ridge regression between two frozen encoders locate and orient the mapping simultaneously, and a classifier fitted only on report text then predicts findings from the mapped images. In each frame, AbacusGS sorts only the visible boxes, and one dot product per box decides whether the box is read forward or backward. A short order-aware fine-tuning converts an existing 3DGS model, and the over operator of 3DGS stays unchanged. On 13 standard scenes, AbacusGS loses 0.13 dB PSNR on average against an equally fine-tuned 3DGS model. In an OpenGL viewer that orders splats on the CPU, AbacusGS renders frames 4.5 times faster than per-splat sorting. We also present a compact format of 17 bytes per splat and a CUDA tile renderer that use the same order. The code will be released.

arXiv:2611.18244v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Efficient sequential recommendation has emerged as a promising paradigm for providing real-time personalized service. To deploy models under resource-constrained environment, model compression becomes a necessity, yet existing methods typically apply uniform compression ratios, overlooking the heterogeneity in user intent complexity. This "one-size-fits-all" approach leads to a fundamental Capacity-Complexity Mismatch, where computational resources are either wasted on simple instances or insufficient for complex ones. To address this, we propose RACE (Ranking-uncertainty Aware Capacity-Adaptive Customization for Efficient Sequential Recommendation), a framework that dynamically adapts both model structures and input sequences with uncertainty-aware compression ratios. To ensure capacity-adaptive inference, RACE captures the model's intrinsic uncertainty of its predictions and transforms it into a proactive resource allocator. Specifically, we derive a list-wise ranking-uncertainty metric from the distributional stability of top-$K$ predictions, which serves as a measurable proxy for instance complexity. A lightweight predictor is then trained via self-supervision to anticipate this uncertainty from early-layer features. Guided by this signal, RACE performs instance-specific slimming in two dimensions: a hypernetwork-style channel sensitivity extractor identifies parameter redundancy, while importance-aware progressive sequence filtering mitigates data redundancy. Extensive experiments on four popular datasets demonstrate that RACE outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on accuracy, efficiency, and adaptability.

A common property of their equations of motion is that the inertia matrix is a constant matrix, there are no nonlinear velocity terms, and the gravity term contains simple nonlinear terms. By performing a Taylor expansion of the gravity term and making a linear approximation, it is easy to derive a linearized model, and calculations for future states or walkability determination can be performed instantaneously without the need for numerical integration. This paper extends the method to a planar biped robot model with knees. First, we derive the equations of motion, constraint conditions, and inelastic collisions for a planar 6-DOF biped robot, design its control system, and numerically generate a stable bipedal gait on a horizontal plane. Next, we reduce the equations of motion to a 3-DOF model, and derive a linearized model by approximating the gravity term as linear around the expansion point for the thigh frame angle. Through numerical simulations, we demonstrate that calculations for future states and walkability determination can be completed in negligible time. By applying control inputs to the obtained model, performing state-space realization, and then discretizing it, instantaneous walkability determination through iterative calculation becomes possible. Through detailed gait analysis, we discuss how the knee joint flexion angle and the expansion point affect the accuracy of the linear approximation, and the issues that arise when descending a small step.

We present NovoCRF, a conditional random field (CRF) whose states are prefix masses, so that its paths are exactly the peptides within $\pm$0.06 Da of the precursor mass. A small network scores each edge from physics-derived ion-match features and is trained with its scores globally normalized over all mass-feasible peptides. To our knowledge, NovoCRF is the first de novo method trained with exact normalization over all mass-feasible peptides. Our model has 3.6M parameters and trains in about 27 GPU-hours. Because it is small, NovoCRF can also adapt to each run at inference time: it fine-tunes part of its weights on the run's own confident answers, recalibrates the run's precursor and fragment masses, and uses retention time, predicted with a pretrained indexed-retention-time model, as further evidence. On nine held-out data-dependent acquisition datasets, NovoCRF has the highest peptide recall on five, and the transformer model InstaNovo on the other four. Where the spectrum determines the peptide, on labels with at most one peptide bond without a b or y ion, NovoCRF outperforms RNovA, $\pi$-PrimeNovo and CasanovoV5 on every dataset and InstaNovo on six of nine. The transformer models lead where many fragment ions are missing, and there their recall is up to 29 points higher on peptides of their own training data than on other peptides, while NovoCRF's recall differs least between seen and unseen peptides. NovoCRF also searches modifications it was never trained on at their exact mass: on a public spike-in of peptides with non-natural residues it finds 69.2% of the labeled spectra, against 64.4% for RNovA. With a GPU it sequences 203 spectra/s in its default two passes, and on the CPU alone it still sequences 67 spectra/s.

arXiv:2611.22546v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: The spectrum of artificial atoms coupled to resonators in the ultrastrong coupling regime have been analyzed using the quantum Rabi model over a wide range of coupling strengths. However, the accuracy of models obtained by truncating multilevel artificial atoms to two levels, as well as the correspondence between effective parameters extracted from spectral fitting and the bare parameters of the circuit Hamiltonian, depends on the multilevel structure of the system. In this study, I analyze the spectrum of an ultrastrongly coupled circuit consisting of a multilevel superconducting artificial atom and a resonator using a circuit Hamiltonian, and investigate the effects of truncating higher atomic levels on the low-energy spectrum. Based on L\"owdin partitioning, I evaluate the contributions of virtual transitions through higher atomic levels and show that diagonal energy corrections reduce the errors arising from simple two-level truncation over a wide parameter range. I also show that there are parameter regimes in which readjustment of the effective Rabi parameters successfully reproduces the multilevel spectrum, while systematic deviations remain in other regimes. These results demonstrate the necessity of separately evaluating two-level truncation, perturbative corrections, and effective-parameter fitting in ultrastrongly coupled systems, and provide guidance for quantitative spectral analysis of multilevel quantum circuits.

arXiv:2611.22530v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Targeted recovery in modular quantum processors requires identifying the component affected by a fault. Independent qubits can monitor faults through repeated preparation and measurement. Bell-pair probes improve the guaranteed correct-site probability for unknown local channels, but require partners kept away from the fault. Can entanglement among exposed probes supply this advantage without protected storage? We establish a quantum-code criterion for optimal distributed fault sensing of one unknown local qubit channel with strength in a prescribed positive range. For one interrogation with zero false alarms and no background noise, suitable code states attain the optimal worst-case correct-site probability, improving on independent probes by 50% with every qubit exposed. Exact attainment is equivalent to mutually orthogonal input and single-qubit Pauli error subspaces. Pairwise entanglement gives no improvement, and entanglement depth at most four cannot exceed 95.54% of the optimum without protected ancillas. Approaching the optimum without protected ancillas also requires a number of probes proportional to the array size to participate in larger entangled factors. For a persistent fault under memoryless depolarizing background of fixed strength 0 < eta < 1, independent probes already attain the optimal logarithmic interrogation scaling at fixed success between zero and one and a positive false-alarm budget. In three 1000-site comparisons with specified readouts, an encoded-probe protocol certifies fewer interrogations than independent probes and only one more than optimally decoded ideal Bell pairs, while storing no protected qubits.

ReShap extracts compact feature representations from raw image observations, performs SHAP-based feature attribution to characterize how each feature contributes to the policy's decisions, and distills the deep RL policy into an interpretable surrogate trained on the full set of (state, policy-action) pairs along the policy's visited distribution. We instantiate the surrogate with three interpretable model families (decision trees, linear regression, and logistic regression) and compare their fidelity and task return. We evaluate ReShap on Atari and Box2D environments using three deep RL algorithms and conduct a human-subject study to assess the clarity and trustworthiness of the resulting policies. Results show that ReShap preserves competitive task performance, that decision trees generally outperform linear and logistic regression, and that linear regression is weakest in most settings.

arXiv:2611.01074v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Cross-view object geo-localization (CVOGL) aims to identify a query-view target in a satellite image, yet reliable instance grounding remains challenging under substantial viewpoint discrepancies. Although recent methods incorporate multimodal prompts, they insufficiently address the varying transferability of linguistic and visual evidence across views. Viewpoint-dependent descriptions (e.g., building facades visible in oblique UAV views but not in top-down satellite images) may become unreliable for satellite grounding, while visually similar instances further complicate target identification. To address these challenges, we rethink CVOGL from a visual grounding perspective and propose GAV (Grounding Across Views), a view-aware framework for constructing target-centered evidence and establishing discriminative cross-view correspondence. Specifically, view-aware referring reasoning mitigates viewpoint-dependent ambiguity, multi-token exemplar prompting and contrastive alignment strengthen visual-semantic correspondence, and scene-level supervision with alignment-based verification distinguishes competing satellite instances. We further introduce CVOGL-Text, a street- and drone-to-satellite benchmark with query-derived expressions. GAV achieves state-of-the-art performance on MoP-UAV with 62.55% Acc@0.5 (+18.19 percentage points) and outperforms evaluated click-point baselines on CVOGL-Text.

We define two notions of separability relative to an experiment, one on either side of separability. Inner separability confines the local states to the preparable sets. Outer separability lets the local factors be self-adjoint operators positive on the available effects but not necessarily positive semidefinite. We find exactly when each departs from separability and that outer separability keeps the operational content of separability for the available measurements: outer separable states, entangled or not, admit local hidden variable models for every behaviour these measurements generate and, when the steered party is unrestricted, local hidden state models for every assemblage the steering party's measurements generate. Such hidden state models do not imply outer separability in general, but we identify conditions under which they do.

We hypothesize that broader semantic context can be more reliably captured from EEG than individual sentences. Accordingly, EEG representations are first classified into semantic classes, which are defined as groups of related sentences, followed by sentence retrieval within the predicted class. Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.14912v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models trained with Reinforcement Learning (RL) with verifiable rewards exhibit strong reasoning ability and broad generalization, whereas models trained with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) are often viewed as more prone to memorization and limited transfer. This paper rethinks this distinction through the lens of SFT training data on widely used Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 series models. First, we study the role of data source and show that it is critical: a carefully mixed SFT dataset substantially outperforms data generated solely by a larger model. Second, we study the role of data scale and show that matching the number of correct rollouts between SFT and RL greatly improves SFT generalization, while matching the total rollout budget enables SFT to generalize as well as RL. Combining these two factors further enables SFT to generalize even better than RL. Third, by using LLM annotations to characterize the solution methods in training rollouts, we show that larger datasets cover more tail methods and that these tail methods provide generalizable reasoning signals. Finally, we support these empirical findings theoretically by analyzing the training dynamics of shallow transformers under both RL and SFT.

arXiv:2603.04760v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modular reconfigurable robots require reliable mechanisms for automated tool exchange, but conventional rigid active couplings often fail due to inevitable positioning and orientational errors. To address this, we propose a misalignment-tolerant tool changer. The tool changer consists of an insert part on the robot side, which contains a servo-driven cam and lock-pin, and a receptacle part on the tool side, which has an isosceles triangular lead-in guide and chamfered walls. During insertion, these geometries generate angled contact forces that passively align the two parts, so the tool changer compensates for angular and lateral misalignments without force sensors. A motor-driven rotating tool exchange station stores the tools and rotates to bring the selected tool to the exchange position. Experiments confirmed that, with the current guide and chamfer geometry, the tool changer tolerates rotational offsets of $ \pm$ 20 degrees and lateral offsets of up to 7 mm.

Agentic frameworks further advance this direction by decoupling explicit game logic and controllable world representations from visual generation. However, existing approaches support only simple game settings and predefined motion patterns, generalize poorly to unseen environments and characters, and offer limited real-time interactivity. In this paper, we introduce Wizard, an agentic game world model that enables real-time, precise control over character motions while generalizing zero-shot across novel scenes, characters, and actions. To achieve this, we construct a diverse dataset spanning 805 scenes and 178 characters, incorporating skeleton and geometry information as structured proxies to condition video generation. Our agentic framework explicitly tracks and updates game states to support character-aware adaptive masking and world-anchored spatial conditioning, improving character identity preservation and spatial consistency. Experiments on WBench show that our method achieves higher gameplay fidelity with comparable video quality and spatiotemporal consistency, while using fewer parameters and less training data than state-of-the-art world models. These advantages are also retained in our two-step real-time variant. Overall, Wizard combines agentic control with structured proxy-based generation to enable player-driven game creation with real-time, generalizable, and mechanically consistent world simulation.

Practitioners therefore edit their RMs, but they learn whether an edit works only after an RL run. We show that the response of a policy to an RM edit can be forecast before training, from samples of the current policy and the scores of the old and fresh RM. If we read the RM as a set of prices, the first-order theory of KL-regularized RL implies that each feature moves in proportion to its within-prompt covariance with the change in reward. We implant controlled price changes into retrained RMs under a 2^(4-1) fractional factorial design with a self-distilled placebo, run 54 RL runs from six parent policies, and fix every forecast before the runs. With the covariance predictor, we predict the direction of all 20 changes in supply whose forecast has the same sign at every parent and explain 82% of the standardized change. With counterfactual prices, the classical alternative, we explain 50%. The forecast also holds under GRPO and for real RM upgrades, where we explain 66% out of sample with a coefficient frozen from the factorial runs. For rent, the gap between the proxy reward and a gold reward from stronger judges, we rank RM edits correctly with the same covariance over the first 30 steps (Spearman 0.94). This measures the horizon of the forecast: by step 200, the ranking of the factorial edits reverses under both RLOO and GRPO, while the real upgrades keep their order. When we vary the KL coefficient beta, the initial response does not depend on beta, and the response saturates below the KL equilibrium. In one experiment, the long-run response to a price rise is consistent with an additional implicit regularizer beta_0 of about 0.003 to 0.007.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2603.04757v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modular robots can adapt their morphology to diverse tasks, but locomotion can impose large loads on detachable joints. This paper presents an NSGA-III-based multi-objective gait optimization framework with three objectives: a locomotion speed, a static stability, and a normalized joint-load metric based on joint reaction forces. The framework yields nondominated gait candidates that reveal the trade-offs among these objectives. In a flat-terrain comparison using the 6-legged tetrapod gait, adding the joint-load objective reduced the mean maximum joint reaction force by 11.5% and increased the mean minimum stability by 41.2%, while decreasing the mean forward speed by 10.5%. Simulations under flat, slope, and step conditions highlighted that locomotion feasibility depended on the combination of robot configuration, gait, and terrain. In physical experiments, the 4-legged trot completed locomotion on flat terrain and a 10 degrees slope, whereas the 6-legged tetrapod and tripod completed locomotion on flat terrain. These results demonstrate the feasibility of joint-load-aware gait generation based on explicit trade-offs among the three evaluated quantities.
