Sources indicate that arXiv:2610.39857v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Automated animal re-identification from photograph sequences can facilitate minimally invasive Capture-Mark-Recapture studies at scale. Yet, photographs taken during an observation session can vary greatly in quality, not always providing the necessary information for accurate re-identification. In this paper, we present latest methods for open-set re-identification from image sequences. We train and evaluate taxonomic classification, sex determination and reidentification models on a dataset of 35,914 photographs of 474 individual seahorses observed in the wild. Combining the photographs of an observation improves all three tasks. For species and sex, a linear probe on DINOv3 embeddings classifies each photograph, and we average the logits over the photographs of an observation. At the observation level, this model reaches a balanced accuracy of 0.97 for species and 0.90 for sex. For open-set re-identification, a fine-tuned MiewID descriptor retrieves candidate individuals, and a learned relevance score weights each photograph. Local feature matching with ALIKED and LightGlue combined with a geometric check with RANSAC that keeps only the consistent matches then reranks the candidates. A logistic model estimates the probability that the individual is already in the gallery. A maximum a posteriori rule then chooses between the best-matching identity and a new individual. This method reaches a normalized accuracy of 0.90 when the gallery holds every past observation of each individual, and 0.83 when it holds only one.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.09670v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Robots increasingly strategy by searching against a reward model learned from human preferences. We measure what this search does to the true objective. On HalfCheetah and Hopper with crowd-sourced labels, and on Meta-World drawer-open and plate-slide with synthetic and blind human labels, harder MPPI search cuts true return by up to 76% while held-out label accuracy stays at 0.75-0.97; with human labels the drawer opens in 0 of 20 runs, against 10 of 10 for the cloned policy the planner starts from. The effect persists with a learned dynamics model and an image scorer. We prove that $\chi^2$-regularized MPPI at a temperature set by the scorer's error spread on the proposals is worst-case optimal, and that no gain can be certified once that spread exceeds the scorer's own. Calibrated from 100 ranked proposal pairs, this rule is the safest fix we test, keeping 86-94% of the cloned policy's return on drawer-open and plate-slide.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (235 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.22428v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: We propose a method towards demonstrating a quantum superposition of a massive mechanical resonator without the need for exact ground-state cooling, a requirement that becomes increasingly difficult to satisfy for low-frequency resonators. Our scheme relies on coupling the resonator to a spin-qubit. Using magnetic force coupling between the motion of the mechanical resonator and the spin-qubit, the resonator is forced into attracted and repelled states as the spin-qubit is coherently controlled. Interference between the resonator states can be observed when a series of $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$-pulses is applied to the spin-qubit within the coherence time of the resonator. The protocol describes a true which-path interference experiment suitable for use at ultra-low temperatures, since it requires only three $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$-pulses, separated in time by half a mechanical period, thus minimizing the heat-load and duration of the experiment. By analysing the experimental requirements necessary to successfully execute the protocol, we show that the protocol is suitable for resonators in a broad regime of resonance frequencies, ranging from 1kHz resonators, which have the advantage of a relatively high spin-coupling, to resonators of more than 100kHz, whose mechanical mode is easier to cool. We show that interference remains visible for resonator mode occupations exceeding 10 phonons. Lastly, we observe that an implementation of the protocol with low-frequency mechanical resonators provides a promising approach towards testing objective collapse models.

Latest Update: NestRL: A Nested Training Regime for Mutual Adaptation in Human-AI Teaming

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (196 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

According to recent reports, arXiv:2602.17737v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mutual adaptation is a central challenge in human-AI teaming, as humans naturally adjust their strategies in response to an AI agent's behavior. Existing approaches attempt to approximate human behavior by diversifying training partners; however, these partners are typically static and fail to capture the adaptive nature of human teammates. When agents are trained jointly in standard multi-agent settings, they often converge to opaque coordination strategies that work only with their co-trained partners, leading to poor generalization. To model adaptive human behavior, we formulate human-AI teaming as an Interactive Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (I-POMDP). We propose NestRL, a nested training regime that learns the solution to a finite-level I-POMDP by training agents at each level against adaptive agents from the level below. This exposes agents to adaptive behavior while preventing emergence of opaque coordination strategies. We provide theoretical analysis showing that NestRL agents avoid convergence to partner-specific strategies, and validate this empirically in the Overcooked domain against state-of-the-art baselines. NestRL achieves higher task performance with both unseen adaptive agents and real human teammates, while exhibiting significantly greater adaptability over the course of interaction.

arXiv:2611.06518v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has advanced generative model post-training in verifiable domains such as code and mathematics, but evaluating video quality, especially emotional expression, often depends on subjective aesthetics and has no uniquely correct target. Existing approaches typically rely on fixed rewards for visual quality, motion quality, and text alignment that poorly capture emotional intent and can invite reward hacking, while RLHF is difficult to scale and subject to individual aesthetic differences that complicate the calibration of facial, body motion, and chromatic cues across narrative contexts. We introduce EmoReward, a new self-evolving training mechanism that distills evidence reliability from reward traces collected during an actual training run to adaptively guide multi-reward weight allocation in subsequent training by determining which emotional evidence to trust and how much to weight it. EmoReward first intends specific grounding cues from the emotional prompt to guide evaluation, then uses heterogeneous signal primitives to score the generated video during the act stage. Reflective Reward Gating calibrates their contributions through instance-level gates for phase, face confidence, conflict, and subtlety, then renormalizes weights over the active set to produce the sample's fused reward. RewardMemory then estimates each primitive's reliability from rollout scores and outcomes within each emotional regime in the finished training run, then fixes bounded multipliers that calibrate fusion weights in the next training run without updating reward models. Experiments on HunyuanVideo 1.5 show improvements across multiple RL algorithms and compare EmoReward with other agentic reward methods under SAGE-GRPO. Ablations and transfer experiments on SD 3.5 and FLUX further support adaptive reward calibration for visual generation.

arXiv:2610.38774v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Similar tongue findings can accompany different syndromes in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), with decisive symptoms absent from the photograph. We present a framework for tongue assessment in which image and pulse findings guide targeted symptom inquiry and acquired answers refine the syndrome shortlist before reporting. Image/pulse predictions guide selection from a sourced symptom question bank. Known answers upgrade the assessment used to select the next question. A calibrated loss of support for the initial prediction triggers reassessment; a subsequent report requires fresh answers supporting a stable candidate. Question and answer records make these decisions inspectable. We construct 2,600 cases from distinct real tongue photographs, assigned syndromes, simulated symptom responses and rendered pulses; 2,599 enter five-fold source-disjoint evaluation and one is training-only. On clean images, image/pulse prediction alone achieves 46.4% fine-syndrome accuracy. At acquisition cost 12, inquiry without image/pulse evidence reaches 34.4%, whereas their combination reaches 65.8% accuracy and 90.8% top-three inclusion. A same-prior, training-optimized static order reaches 59.4% and 87.3%, respectively. In a 200-case visual-training intervention within the same bank, the first question changes in 46.7% of cases and the inquiry NLL-cost curve improves. Component comparisons distinguish these acquisition gains from the coverage-cost tradeoff of reassessment. These controlled results support image-guided acquisition of missing symptoms for ranked TCM decision support.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.22412v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: Encoded fusion combines probabilistic physical fusions to perform a logical Bell measurement. Adaptive choices depend on earlier measurement outcomes and therefore require multiple measurement rounds. We determine the minimum worst-case number of rounds for perfect fusion of two blocks of an irreducible [[n,1]] stabilizer code. A strategy is perfect if the logical Bell measurement succeeds on every branch containing at least one successful physical fusion. Even after fixing the past history, including measurement values, we consider all success/failure branches, including those with zero probability for a particular input state or measurement device. In a lossless model with fixed coordinate pairing, arbitrary Pauli failure bases, and each pair fused exactly once, the optimum equals the minimum root eccentricity over the local complementation orbit of rooted graphs representing the code. The lower bound applies to arbitrary perfect strategies that choose batches and bases using previous outcomes. We also characterize the batch sequences that can occur on an all-failure branch of a perfect strategy by a necessary and sufficient graph adjacency condition. A matching strategy fuses distance layers from the outside in and, after the first success, completes the remaining fusions in at most one further round by changing the failure bases along an induced path.

arXiv:2610.38754v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Knowledge-guided multimodal systems need a way to measure how supplied knowledge affects predictions, including when that knowledge is wrong. Alpha-TCM addresses this problem for traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) through an implemented workflow that separates measurements, supplied knowledge, predictions, and reviewer decisions. Observations and contextual knowledge enter separately, and a replaceable prior allows controlled interventions with fixed modality encoders. Bayesian committee accounting removes the reference prior already contained in each encoder before inserting contextual knowledge. A fully simulated confirmation study uses ten paired seeds and four training sizes. Knowledge context reduces prediction error relative to knowledge-free fusion at 600 and 1,200 training cases; equal-information learned context is competitive at 600 and has lower error at larger sizes. Controlled corruption identifies overconfident and displaced priors as the most damaging challenges. Case-level conflict detection remains weak, and training-time prior regularisation shows no consistent benefit. Functional tests verify the connected workflow separately from predictive performance. The simulation demonstrates how Alpha-TCM measures knowledge dependence, separates it from gains due to additional context, and exposes harmful prior assumptions before clinical evaluation.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.22391v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH) provides a central framework for understanding thermalization in isolated quantum systems. Recently, the infinite-temperature ETH has been established for almost all Floquet eigenstates in linear feedback shift register quantum circuits. Here we introduce brickwork Clifford circuits with $L$ qubits where the induced transformation of Pauli operators is represented by an irreducible symplectic matrix over the finite field $\mathbb F_2$ of the maximal order $2^L+1$, known as a Singer cycle. For these Singer-cycle Clifford circuits, we prove a strong version of ETH: all Floquet eigenstates are thermal at infinite temperature without exceptions. We derive uniform bounds on both diagonal deviations from thermal expectation values and off-diagonal matrix elements of arbitrary observables supported on a fixed number of sites. The results indicate that long-time averages of observables approach the infinite-temperature values in the thermodynamic limit for arbitrary initial states. We also show that the temporal fluctuation of expectation values of observables is exponentially suppressed in the thermodynamic limit, implying that each observable remains close to the infinite-temperature value for almost all times.
